newsitem.title: FRANCE: Calls for war and peace ring out in Corsica.
newsitem.headline: Calls for war and peace ring out in Corsica.

text.p: Conflicting calls for war and peace rang out on the French Mediterranean island of Corsica on Thursday after Prime Minister Alain Juppe vowed to crush separatists who bombed his mayoral office in Bordeaux.

The separatist group Fronte Ribellu (Rebel Front) called on the 250,000 islanders to rise up against French "aggressors", whom they branded "the hereditary enemy" in a statement sent to a news agency in Bastia.
It threatened to kill anyone who assisted police in the crackdown promised by Juppe against the separatists.
The group is regarded to be close to the hardline Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC)-Historic Wing which claimed responsibility for the weekend attack on Juppe's office.
At the same time, a moderate nationalist leader called on Corsicans to unite in a "day for peace" to restore dialogue broken in a standoff between Paris and the guerrillas.
Gilbert Casanova, head of the Ajaccio chamber of commerce and a leader of the Movement for Self-Determination (MPA), said repression would not end violence on the island.
"(Juppe's) declaration of war, intended to reassure Corsicans, will not solve Corsica's political problem," he said, urging all islanders, including guerrillas, to demonstrate for peace.
"Time is running out. We have to find a solution by the end of this year," he told Reuters in an interview.

FLNC hardliners, accusing Juppe of reneging on promises made in secret talks, have launched a new escalation in the cycle of violence and repression that has marked the 21-year-old Corsican separatist movement.
France has put its top anti-terrorist judge in charge of the probe into the Bordeaux bombing and the government has vowed to lock up the guerrillas, publicly branded as terrorists.
Security has been stepped up in major French cities amid fears that the guerrillas may strike again on the mainland.

Two activists of another separatist movement, the Corsican Nationalist Alliance (ANC), were placed under investigation overnight after police found an arsenal of pistols and rifles at their homes on Monday.
Police said they had detained two other Corsicans in the Riviera capital of Nice late last month as they prepared to board a ferry for the island with machineguns in their car.
But police acknowledge the FLNC guerrillas, hardened by two decades of violence and protected by the islanders' tradition of not cooperating with police, will be a tough nut to crack.

"Repression will not solve the problem, even if one can understand the attitude of the prime minister after he was targeted (by the guerillas)," Casanova, who heads the Ajaccio Chamber of Commerce, said.
"It's up to the Corsicans to work for dialogue, but it will take time," he said, adding his "day for peace" proposal could be supported by the bishop of Ajaccio, Andre Lacrampe.
Casanova said dialogue with the government was possible but should be open, unlike the secret talks that were reported to have taken place earlier this year.
The separatists demand greater autonomy rather than total independence from France, a highly centralised state.
Casanova said the talks should cover official recognition of the Corsican people if this were supported by all the islanders.
France's Constitutional Council watchdog has in the past rejected recognition of Corsicans as a distinct people, saying it ran counter to the country's constitution.
